### `README.md`

# PEFT Ranking Across Indic Script Families

> Final project overview for the IndicXNLI PEFT study, including the primary LoRA/DoRA/IA³ sweep and the hybrid IA³+LoRA follow-up.

## Current status

This repository contains the full reproducible study and the final comparison workflow.
The primary analysis is the validation-set study in notebooks 00–06, while notebooks
07–10 cover held-out test evaluation and the hybrid method comparison.

The authoritative interpretation is in [docs/validated-results.md](docs/validated-results.md).
The project history and continuation notes are in [docs/PROJECT_STATUS.md](docs/PROJECT_STATUS.md).

## Primary findings

### 1) Primary validation-set results (source of truth for the main study)

These are the validated results from the main LoRA/DoRA/IA³ sweep on the validation split.
They are not the held-out test-set results.

| Budget | Hindi winner | Telugu winner |
|-------:|-------------|--------------|
|     50 | DoRA        | DoRA         |
|    100 | DoRA        | IA³          |
|    500 | IA³         | IA³          |
|  1,000 | IA³         | IA³          |
|  2,000 | IA³         | IA³          |
| 20,000 | IA³         | LoRA         |

Important: this table reflects the main validation analysis only. See
[docs/validated-results.md](docs/validated-results.md) for the supported claims,
caveats, and limitations.

### 2) Hybrid comparison on the held-out test set

This is a separate analysis that compares the hybrid IA³+LoRA method against the best
primary method for each budget-language cell.

The final notebook is [notebooks/10-final-comparison.ipynb](notebooks/10-final-comparison.ipynb).
The generated comparison outputs are in [results/10-final-comparison](results/10-final-comparison).

Verified head-to-head result on the test set:

- Hybrid wins 8/12 budget-language cells
- Win rate: 67%
- Wins occur at budgets 100, 500, 2000, and 20000 in both languages
- Losses occur at budget 50 and budget 1000 in both languages
- The 50-budget loss is collapse-driven; the 1000-budget loss is a real IA³-specific effect

This is a separate, test-set result. It should not be mixed with the validation-set table above.

- The primary sweep uses validation data for learning-rate selection and is

  a pairwise significance result.

  asset; the project depends on the preserved saved experiment outputs and
  notebook-generated artifacts.

### `docs/report-materials/abstract-and-limitations.md`

> **Status notice (2026-08-24):** This is an earlier draft. Its universal IA³
> ranking claim and its 13-run collapse count conflict with the current validated
> primary results. Do not use it as the final abstract; see
> `../validated-results.md` and the files under `results/`.

Abstract

We investigate whether the relative performance ranking of three parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods — LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ — holds across script families and training-data budgets, extending prior comparisons that were limited to Latin-script languages at a single fixed dataset size. Using XLM-RoBERTa-base fine-tuned on IndicXNLI, we evaluate all three methods on Hindi (Devanagari, Indo-Aryan) and Telugu (Telugu script, Dravidian) across six budgets (50 to 20,000 examples) and three random seeds (108 total configurations). We find that IA³ consistently outperforms LoRA and DoRA once training data exceeds 500 examples, in both languages — a crossover that replicates across two typologically distinct scripts — while LoRA and DoRA remain statistically indistinguishable from one another at every budget tested. IA³'s advantage is accompanied by higher variance at the smallest budgets (50–100 examples), where 9 of 108 runs failed to exceed random-chance accuracy. These results suggest PEFT method rankings are not universal across data regimes, and that recommendations should be conditioned on annotation budget rather than treated as fixed.

Limitations
Capped "high-resource" budget. The largest training budget used (20,000 examples) is a compute-constrained substitute for the full IndicXNLI training set (~392,702 examples per language). Whether the observed IA³ advantage persists, narrows, or reverses at true full-data scale is untested. Any reference to "high-resource" or "large-budget" performance in this work should be read as bounded by 20,000 examples, not the complete dataset.
Pooled, not per-language, hyperparameter search. Learning rates were selected once per method using data pooled across both languages, rather than tuned separately per language. This was a deliberate methodological choice to prevent language-specific LR tuning from confounding the cross-language ranking comparison — the central question this study addresses. A consequence is that reported performance for each method may not represent that method's absolute best-achievable result in either language individually.
Small-budget instability, concentrated in IA³. 13 of 108 runs (12%) failed to exceed random-chance accuracy; 9 of these occurred in IA³ at the two smallest budgets (50 and 100 examples). We attribute this to IA³'s selected learning rate (5×10⁻³) being fifty times larger than LoRA/DoRA's (1×10⁻⁴), which appears to occasionally destabilize training when very few gradient-informative examples are available. These runs are retained in the reported means and confidence intervals rather than discarded, so budget-500 and below results for IA³ should be read with this variance in mind (full listing in results/collapsed_runs.csv).
Two languages, two methods' worth of adapters. Findings are drawn from one Indo-Aryan and one Dravidian language, both processed through the same multilingual encoder (XLM-RoBERTa-base) and the same NLI task (IndicXNLI). Generalization to other Indic languages, other script families, other base encoders, or other task types (e.g., generation, sequence labeling) is not established by this study.
Classification head shared across methods. All three PEFT configurations train the same randomly initialized classification head alongside their respective adapters (modules_to_save=["classifier"]). It remains possible that this shared, jointly-trained component compresses differences between methods that would otherwise be more visible — particularly relevant to the null result between LoRA and DoRA — and this was not isolated as a separate experimental factor.
Single base model. All experiments use XLM-RoBERTa-base exclusively. Method rankings observed here may not transfer to larger multilingual encoders, decoder-only architectures, or encoders with different multilingual pretraining compositions.


### `docs/report-materials/introduction.md`

> **Status notice (2026-08-24):** This is an earlier draft written before the
> final validated results and the current repo layout were adopted. It should not
> be used as the final report text. See `../validated-results.md` and the current
> `README.md` for the authoritative findings and file structure.

Introduction

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods — LoRA (Hu et al., 2021), its variant DoRA (Liu et al., 2024), and IA³ (Liu et al., 2022) — have become the default approach for adapting large pretrained language models to downstream tasks under limited compute and memory budgets. Each modifies a frozen backbone differently: LoRA injects low-rank additive updates into attention weight matrices; DoRA decomposes those updates into separate magnitude and direction components, aiming to more closely approximate full fine-tuning's learning dynamics; IA³ instead learns a small number of per-layer rescaling vectors, updating far fewer parameters than either LoRA variant. Comparative studies of these methods typically report a fixed ranking — usually favoring LoRA or DoRA — but this ranking is generally established under a single, specific experimental condition: one dataset size, one language, one script.

Two recent comparative studies (Frontiers in Big Data, 2025; PROPOR, 2026) evaluate LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ against one another, but share two limitations relevant to this work. First, both restrict their language coverage to Latin-script languages — English and Brazilian Portuguese — leaving open whether their reported method rankings hold for languages with different scripts, morphological structures, and tokenization behavior under multilingual encoders. Second, both evaluate at a single fixed training-set size, leaving open whether the reported ranking is a property of the methods themselves or an artifact of the particular data regime tested. Given that annotation budgets in real-world low-resource NLP settings routinely range from tens to tens of thousands of examples, a ranking established at one dataset size provides limited guidance for practitioners operating anywhere else on that spectrum.

This gap is particularly consequential for Indic languages. India's official languages span multiple distinct script families and language families — Devanagari and Indo-Aryan (e.g., Hindi), Telugu script and Dravidian (e.g., Telugu), among others — and multilingual encoders such as XLM-RoBERTa are known to tokenize these languages with substantially different subword fragmentation rates than English, which can affect how efficiently PEFT adapters exploit a fixed effective sequence length. Whether a PEFT method ranking derived from English/Portuguese evaluation transfers to this setting is an empirical question, not a safe assumption.

We address this gap directly. Using XLM-RoBERTa-base fine-tuned on IndicXNLI, we compare LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ on two Indic languages selected specifically for their script and family contrast — Hindi (Devanagari, Indo-Aryan) and Telugu (Telugu script, Dravidian) — across six training budgets spanning three orders of magnitude (50 to 20,000 examples) and three random seeds, for a total of 108 trained configurations. This design lets us ask two questions no prior study has answered jointly: (1) does the relative ranking of these three PEFT methods change as annotation budget changes, and (2) does whatever ranking emerges hold consistently across two languages from different script families, or is it script-dependent? Our results (Section [Results]) show a clear, budget-dependent, and cross-script-consistent ranking — IA³ outperforms both LoRA and DoRA once training data exceeds roughly 500 examples, in both languages — challenging the assumption that a PEFT method ranking established under one language and one data regime generalizes broadly.

## Key PROPOR 2026 finding — directly comparable to your LoRA≈DoRA result

Their paper states explicitly: **"DoRA offers no practical advantages over LoRA, matching its performance at the cost of a 28% increase in training time"** (BERTimbau-Large, high LR). Exact numbers: LoRA F1=81.32 vs. DoRA F1=80.61–81.22 (essentially tied), while DoRA took noticeably longer (e.g., 02:40:52 vs. 01:23:41 at 2 epochs — roughly double, not just 28%, at that specific config, though their headline "28%" figure refers to a different epoch/setting).

**This is a striking, direct confirmation of your own finding** — you independently found LoRA≈DoRA with no meaningful F1 difference, and DoRA being the most compute-expensive of the three methods. Your Discussion section can now cite this as convergent evidence across languages and tasks (Portuguese QA vs. Hindi/Telugu NLI), which meaningfully strengthens your paper.

### `docs/report-materials/related-work.md`

Related Work

Parameter-efficient fine-tuning. LoRA (Hu et al., 2021) is the most widely adopted PEFT method, injecting trainable low-rank matrices into frozen attention projections and requiring only a small fraction of a model's parameters to be updated. DoRA (Liu et al., 2024) extends this by decomposing pretrained weights into magnitude and direction components, updating each separately, with the goal of more closely tracking full fine-tuning's optimization behavior while retaining LoRA's parameter efficiency. IA³ (Liu et al., 2022) takes a distinct approach, learning per-layer rescaling vectors applied to keys, values, and feedforward activations rather than injecting new weight matrices — resulting in substantially fewer trainable parameters than either LoRA variant. These three methods are frequently benchmarked against one another and against full fine-tuning, typically on English-language classification or generation tasks.

PEFT comparison studies. Direct comparisons of LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ have generally been conducted on Latin-script languages at a single fixed training-set size (Frontiers in Big Data, 2025; PROPOR, 2026), reporting a specific method ranking under those conditions. This leaves two open questions our work addresses: whether that ranking is sensitive to the amount of available training data, and whether it is sensitive to the script or morphological structure of the target language. Broader PEFT literature has separately studied data-efficiency effects (comparing PEFT methods at varying dataset sizes within a single language) and cross-lingual transfer effects (comparing a single PEFT method across languages), but to our knowledge these two axes have not been jointly varied in a controlled comparison of LoRA, DoRA, and IA³.

Multilingual encoders and Indic NLP. XLM-RoBERTa (Conneau et al., 2020) is a widely used multilingual encoder pretrained across 100 languages, including Hindi and Telugu, and serves as a common backbone for cross-lingual transfer research. Benchmark suites such as IndicGLUE and IndicXTREME (Kakwani et al., 2020; Doddapaneni et al., 2023) have substantially expanded the availability of labeled evaluation data for Indic languages, including IndicXNLI (Aggarwal et al., 2022), a machine-translated extension of XNLI covering eleven Indic languages including Hindi and Telugu, which we use as the evaluation task in this work. Prior work using these resources has generally focused on establishing baseline model performance or comparing full fine-tuning against zero-shot cross-lingual transfer, rather than comparing PEFT methods against one another within this language setting.

Tokenization and script effects. Subword tokenizers trained primarily on Latin-script, high-resource corpora are known to fragment non-Latin-script and morphologically rich languages into a larger number of subword units per word, which can affect effective sequence length, training efficiency, and downstream task performance. Our own tokenizer fragmentation analysis (Section [Methodology]) quantifies this effect directly for Hindi and Telugu under XLM-RoBERTa's tokenizer, motivating our choice to test PEFT methods on two languages with markedly different fragmentation profiles rather than treating "Indic languages" as a single uniform setting.

Positioning of this work. Unlike prior PEFT comparisons, we vary training budget across three orders of magnitude and evaluate on two languages from different script and language families, allowing us to test whether a PEFT method ranking is a stable property of the methods or contingent on the specific data regime and language under study.

### `docs/report-materials/results-and-discussion.md`

> **Status notice (2026-08-24):** This is an earlier draft and contains values
> and conclusions that do not match the current validated primary results. In
> particular, it overstates IA³'s consistency and undercounts collapsed runs.
> Do not use it as the final Results/Discussion section; see
> `../validated-results.md` and the files under `results/`.

Results

Data-efficiency curves. Figure 1 shows macro F1 as a function of training budget for each PEFT method, plotted separately for Hindi and Telugu. All three methods follow the expected shape — near-chance performance at the smallest budgets (F1 ≈ 0.17–0.22 at 50–100 samples, close to the 0.167 random-chance floor for 3-way classification), rising to substantially above-chance performance at the largest budget tested (F1 = 0.59–0.68 at 20,000 samples).

IA³ consistently outperforms LoRA and DoRA from budget = 500 onward, in both languages. At budget = 500, IA³ reaches F1 = 0.401 (Hindi) and 0.382 (Telugu), compared to F1 ≈ 0.24 for both LoRA and DoRA in both languages — roughly a 0.14–0.16 absolute F1 advantage. This gap persists at every subsequent budget: at 2,000 samples, IA³ leads by 0.22 F1 in Hindi (0.548 vs. 0.321–0.323) and by 0.11–0.14 F1 in Telugu (0.399 vs. 0.284–0.286). At the largest budget (20,000), the gap narrows but IA³ retains a lead in Hindi (0.676 vs. 0.630–0.633) and in Telugu (0.632 vs. 0.587–0.591). Because this ordering holds independently in both Hindi (Indo-Aryan, Devanagari script) and Telugu (Dravidian, Telugu script), the IA³ advantage does not appear to be script-specific — it replicates across two typologically and orthographically distinct languages.

LoRA and DoRA are statistically indistinguishable at every budget tested. Across all twelve (language × budget) cells excluding the two smallest, LoRA and DoRA differ by at most 0.02 F1, and their 95% confidence intervals overlap substantially in every case (e.g., at budget = 20,000, Hindi: LoRA 0.633 ± 0.004 vs. DoRA 0.630 ± 0.002). DoRA's added magnitude-direction decomposition produces no measurable accuracy benefit over plain LoRA in this setting, despite incurring higher trainable-parameter count (906K vs. 888K) and the longest total training time of the three methods (Table 2).

Ranking agreement across languages. Using the best-performing method at each budget as the unit of comparison, IA³ is the top performer at 4 of 6 budgets in both Hindi and Telugu (500, 1000, 2000, and 20000), giving 100% ranking agreement at the budgets where a clear winner emerges. At the two smallest budgets (50, 100), all three methods are statistically indistinguishable from chance and from each other, so no meaningful ranking exists to compare.

Stability at small budgets. IA³'s advantage comes with a caveat: it shows a markedly wider confidence interval at small-to-moderate budgets than LoRA or DoRA — e.g., at Telugu budget = 1000, IA³'s 95% CI is ±0.123 (mean F1 = 0.290) versus ±0.087 for DoRA and ±0.059 for LoRA at the same budget. Of 108 total training runs, 13 (12%) failed to learn entirely (accuracy at exact chance level, 0.333); 9 of these 13 failures occurred in IA³ specifically, concentrated at the 50- and 100-sample budgets. We attribute this to IA³'s selected learning rate (5×10⁻³, chosen by a pooled hyperparameter search) being fifty times larger than LoRA/DoRA's (1×10⁻⁴) — a rate that supports faster adaptation at moderate-to-large budgets but appears to occasionally destabilize training when only 50–100 gradient-informative examples are available.

Compute efficiency. IA³ uses the fewest trainable parameters of the three methods (657K vs. 888K for LoRA and 906K for DoRA) but does not translate this into the fastest wall-clock training time in our implementation, likely reflecting the computational structure of its rescaling operations rather than a fundamental efficiency disadvantage (Table 2, compute_efficiency.csv).

Discussion

The central finding — that IA³ outperforms both LoRA and DoRA once training data exceeds roughly 500 examples, and that this ordering is stable across two languages from different script families — runs counter to the common default of treating LoRA as the safe, general-purpose choice for PEFT. In our setting, IA³'s much smaller set of trainable parameters (rescaling vectors rather than low-rank matrices) appears sufficient, and possibly even advantageous, for adapting a multilingual encoder to a classification task once a moderate amount of task-specific signal is available. This is consistent with the original IA³ paper's motivation — that multiplicative rescaling can be a more parameter-efficient inductive bias than additive low-rank updates for certain adaptation regimes — but to our knowledge this is the first time the comparison has been extended to a non-Latin-script, low-resource Indic setting with a systematic budget sweep.

The absence of any measurable difference between LoRA and DoRA is a notable negative result. DoRA's magnitude-direction decomposition was proposed to improve on LoRA's learning capacity, and prior work reports DoRA advantages on English-centric benchmarks; we do not observe that advantage here. One plausible explanation is that the classification head — not the encoder adapters — is the primary bottleneck at small-to-moderate budgets in our setup (both methods must simultaneously learn a randomly initialized head, discussed further in docs/methodology-notes.md), which may compress any encoder-level differences between LoRA and DoRA that would otherwise be visible.

The instability observed in IA³ at the smallest budgets is worth treating as a substantive finding rather than an artifact to be engineered away. A learning rate tuned for good performance at moderate-to-large budgets (our pooled search selected 5×10⁻³ using budget = 2000 as the representative size) is not guaranteed to be stable at 50–100 samples, where a small number of noisy or unrepresentative gradient steps can dominate training. This suggests that any practical guidance drawn from this study — "IA³ is the strongest PEFT method for Hindi/Telugu NLI" — should be qualified by budget: IA³ appears to be the preferred choice once a few hundred labeled examples are available, but LoRA's comparatively lower variance at 50–100 samples may make it the safer choice in extremely low-resource annotation settings.

Two limitations bound how far these conclusions generalize. First, "high-resource" in this study means 20,000 examples, not the full ~392,702-example training set, for compute reasons documented in docs/methodology-notes.md; whether the IA³ advantage persists, narrows, or reverses at the true full-data scale is untested. Second, learning rates were searched once per method, pooled across both languages, to keep the cross-language comparison uncontaminated by per-language LR tuning — this is methodologically appropriate for our research question but means the reported numbers are not necessarily each method's absolute best-achievable performance in either language individually.


### `docs/validated-results.md`

# Final project results summary

This document consolidates the full evidence from the maintained project: the
primary validation sweep and the later hybrid held-out test comparison. It is
intended to be the one-page summary for reporting and interpretation.

## 1) Scope of the study

The project includes three phases:

1. Primary validation sweep in notebooks `00–06`
2. Held-out test evaluation in notebook `07`
3. Hybrid IA³+LoRA follow-up and final comparison in notebooks `08–10`

The main primary sweep is the validated validation-set experiment. The hybrid
results are a separate follow-up analysis on the held-out test split and are
therefore reported as a distinct comparison, not as a replacement for the
primary validation claims.

## 2) Primary validation-set results (the main study)

The full primary sweep contains 108 validation-set runs:

`3 methods × 2 languages × 6 training budgets × 3 seeds`

The methods are LoRA, DoRA, and IA³. The maintained validation analysis uses
XLM-RoBERTa-base with a trainable classifier head. The pooled search selected
LoRA `1e-4`, DoRA `1e-4`, and IA³ `5e-3`.

### Mean macro-F1 ranking by budget

| Budget | Hindi winner | Telugu winner |
|---:|---|---|
| 50 | DoRA | DoRA |
| 100 | DoRA | IA³ |
| 500 | IA³ | IA³ |
| 1,000 | IA³ | IA³ |
| 2,000 | IA³ | IA³ |
| 20,000 | IA³ | LoRA |

The supported descriptive reading is that IA³ is the highest-mean method at the
intermediate 500–2,000 budgets in both languages, and in all reported Hindi
budgets from 500 onward. It is not correct to claim that IA³ wins every budget
from 500 onward in both languages.

The full primary values are in `results/06-results-analysis/ranking_table.csv`.
The corrected validation summary is in `results/06-results-analysis/summary_with_ci.csv`.

## 3) Held-out test-set comparison and hybrid follow-up

The hybrid IA³+LoRA experiments are kept in the active project tree under:

- `notebooks/08-hybrid-formal.ipynb`
- `notebooks/09-hybrid-test-evaluation.ipynb`
- `notebooks/10-final-comparison.ipynb`
- `results/08 — Hybrid IA3+LoRA/`
- `results/09 — Hybrid test-set eval/`
- `results/10-final-comparison/`

These are follow-on analyses and should be interpreted as a supplemental,
test-set comparison rather than a replacement for the validated primary study.

### Head-to-head result: hybrid vs best primary method

The final comparison uses the tested cells in `results/10-final-comparison/hybrid_vs_best_primary.csv`.
The verified test-set outcome is:

- Hybrid wins 8/12 budget-language cells
- Win rate: 67%
- Wins occur at 100, 500, 2,000, and 20,000 in both languages
- Losses occur at 50 and 1,000 in both languages

This means the hybrid method improves over the best primary approach in the
majority of the held-out test cells.

### Final comparison summary table

| Language | Budget | Best primary | Hybrid | Result |
|---|---:|---:|---:|---|
| Hindi | 50 | 0.2211 (DoRA) | 0.1667 | Loss |
| Hindi | 100 | 0.1987 (LoRA) | 0.2758 | Win |
| Hindi | 500 | 0.3756 (IA³) | 0.4361 | Win |
| Hindi | 1000 | 0.4012 (IA³) | 0.3492 | Loss |
| Hindi | 2000 | 0.4901 (IA³) | 0.5425 | Win |
| Hindi | 20000 | 0.6700 (IA³) | 0.6913 | Win |
| Telugu | 50 | 0.2026 (LoRA) | 0.1667 | Loss |
| Telugu | 100 | 0.2033 (LoRA) | 0.2754 | Win |
| Telugu | 500 | 0.3539 (IA³) | 0.4060 | Win |
| Telugu | 1000 | 0.2635 (IA³) | 0.2577 | Loss |
| Telugu | 2000 | 0.4010 (IA³) | 0.4752 | Win |
| Telugu | 20000 | 0.6280 (LoRA) | 0.6539 | Win |

The complete source data for the final comparison is in
`results/10-final-comparison/`.

## 4) Final interpretation

The project supports a two-level interpretation:

- For the primary validation sweep, IA³ is the strongest mean-performing method at
  the intermediate budgets and is the most defensible main validation result.
- For the held-out test comparison, the hybrid IA³+LoRA method is the stronger
  final test-set approach in the majority of budget-language cells.

Taken together, the strongest overall claim is that the primary validation study
identifies IA³ as the leading baseline family, while the later hybrid test-set
analysis shows that a hybrid IA³+LoRA configuration can improve over the best
primary method in the majority of held-out settings.

## 5) Important caveats

- These are validation-set results for the primary sweep. The available
  `test.parquet` split is not used by the main sweep, and the validation split is
  also used in learning-rate selection.
- `summary_with_ci.csv` uses a two-sided t interval for three seeds (`df=2`,
  `t*=4.302652729`). These intervals describe seed variation, not pairwise
  significance.
- The corrected analysis records 24 of 108 runs (22.2%) at or within 0.001 of
  the one-class chance-accuracy baseline (approximately 0.3333). The collapse
  counts are LoRA 8, DoRA 7, and IA³ 9.
- The hybrid configuration uses a dual-LR setup that was not validated with the
  same LR-search protocol used for the primary methods; that asymmetry should be
  disclosed in any write-up.
- The epoch schedule varies by budget, so training budget and the number of
  optimizer updates are not fully isolated.

This document supersedes older draft claims and is the maintained summary for the
full project evidence set.

This directory contains the validated primary-study summaries used for the final
analysis. `summary_with_ci.csv` uses two-sided 95% t intervals with three seeds
(`df=2`, `t*=4.302652729`). These intervals quantify seed variation and must not
be treated as pairwise significance tests.

`rank_order_changes.csv` records descriptive changes in mean-method order. It
does not establish statistical crossovers.

`collapsed_runs.csv` uses `np.isclose(accuracy, 1/3, atol=0.001)` to include
equivalent constant-class outcomes when the validation labels are not perfectly
balanced.

The main notebook that produced these outputs is `notebooks/06-results-analysis.ipynb`.
Use the environment in `requirements.txt` and the source files under `results/` to
reproduce or extend the analysis. The current interpretation is governed by
`docs/validated-results.md`.

# 06 — Corrected primary-results analysis

This notebook analyzes the completed 108-run primary sweep. It does not train models or include the exploratory hybrid work. Results are validation-set estimates because the same validation split was used in learning-rate selection.
## Reporting guidance

Report these as validation-set means with three-seed t intervals. Do not make test-set, statistical-significance, or confirmed-crossover claims from this notebook. Use a separate held-out test evaluation before finalizing the study.

### `notebooks/08-hybrid-formal.ipynb`

#### Markdown
# 08 — Hybrid IA3+LoRA (fixed)

`get_peft_model(..., IA3Config).add_adapter("lora", LoraConfig)` raises
`ValueError: Cannot combine adapters with different peft types` — a
`PeftModel` is bound to one tuner type, and `PeftMixedModel` does not
support IA3 (checked against installed `peft` — `IA3` is not in
`peft.tuners.mixed.COMPATIBLE_TUNER_TYPES`). This is why the notebook
never ran.

Fix: LoRA goes through `peft` as usual (query/value + classifier via
`modules_to_save`). IA3 is attached **manually** as forward hooks with
plain `nn.Parameter` scaling vectors on `attention.self.key`,
`intermediate.dense`, and `output.dense` — the last one filtered to
exclude `attention.output.dense`, which the original
`target_modules=["...","output.dense"]` matched too via `peft`'s
`endswith` matching, silently pulling attention's output projection
into what the comments called "strictly feedforward" IA3.

Also fixed: original run never called `save_pretrained` — 108→36
comparable adapters were being trained and discarded, leaving no way
to do held-out test evaluation (notebook 09). This version saves
every run and supports resume.

### `notebooks/10-final-comparison.ipynb`
- Cells: 7; code cells: 5; outputs: 1
#### Markdown
# 10 — Final cross-method comparison (test set)

Combines 07's primary-sweep test results (lora/dora/ia3, 108 runs) with 09's
hybrid test results (hybrid_ia3_lora, 36 runs) into one head-to-head comparison.

Unlike 06 (validation set, same split used in LR selection -- caveated there for
exactly that reason), everything here is held-out test performance for every
method. No reuse-in-selection caveat applies to this notebook.

One caveat that *does* still apply: hybrid's epoch schedule was matched to 05's
exactly, but its dual-LR (lora=1e-4, ia3=1e-3, head=1e-4) was a one-shot choice,
not a validated sweep the way 04 found LRs for lora/dora/ia3. Any comparison here
inherits that asymmetry -- disclose it, don't hide it.
## Reporting guidance

Report test macro-F1 means with 3-seed t intervals, same convention as 06.

Hybrid wins at mid-to-large budgets (500-20000) and loses at the two smallest
(50, 1000) -- report both, don't average them into a single "hybrid wins" claim.
The budget=50 loss is a collapse-rate artifact (see `collapsed_runs.csv`); the
budget=1000 loss is not (ia3 alone is unusually stable there) and is worth a
sentence of its own rather than folding into the collapse discussion.

Disclose the LR-search asymmetry noted at the top: lora/dora/ia3 got a validated
LR from 04's sweep, hybrid's dual-LR did not.

I express my sincere gratitude to my faculty advisor, [Faculty Advisor Name], for guidance and constructive feedback throughout this project. I also thank the Department of [Department Name], [University Name], and the open-source research community whose datasets and software made this study possible. I am grateful to my peers and family for their encouragement during the experimental and writing stages.
ABSTRACT
This study examines whether the relative ranking of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods changes with labelled-data availability and remains stable across Indic script families. LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ were adapted to XLM-RoBERTa-base for IndicXNLI classification in Hindi and Telugu. A controlled sweep covered six training budgets (50–20,000 examples), three methods, two languages, and three random seeds, producing 108 validation runs. Mean macro-F1 rankings vary with budget: DoRA leads at 50 examples in both languages, IA³ leads at 500–2,000 examples in both languages and at 20,000 examples in Hindi, while LoRA leads at 20,000 examples in Telugu. Thus, no method is universally best. A separate held-out test follow-up compared a hybrid IA³+LoRA configuration with the best primary method in each cell; the hybrid won 8 of 12 cells. The results support budget-aware PEFT selection, while the small number of seeds, validation-set model selection, and asymmetric hybrid tuning limit inferential claims.

LIST OF ABBREVIATIONS
PEFT — Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning; LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation; DoRA — Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation; IA³ — Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations; NLI — Natural Language Inference; GPU — Graphics Processing Unit.
1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a large pretrained model while leaving most backbone weights frozen. It is attractive when compute, memory, or annotated examples are limited. This motivation for training only a small task-specific parameter set is central to modern PEFT research (Hu et al., 2021; Liu et al., 2022).
1.2 Problem Statement
A PEFT recommendation based on one language and one dataset size may not transfer to a different data regime or script. Existing comparisons seldom vary both axes together in a controlled Indic-language setting. Recent low-resource PEFT studies likewise motivate analysing performance as a function of data availability rather than treating a single benchmark result as universal (Nwaiwu, 2025; Nina et al., 2026).
1.3 Motivation
Hindi and Telugu provide a useful contrast because they differ in script and language family while being evaluated with the same multilingual encoder and task. This makes it possible to investigate whether a ranking is robust or context-dependent. IndicXNLI makes this controlled comparison possible by extending NLI evaluation to Indian languages (Aggarwal et al., 2022).
1.4 Research Questions
This report addresses two research questions:
RQ1: Does the ranking of LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ change as the training-data budget changes?
RQ2: Is the observed ranking consistent for Hindi (Devanagari; Indo-Aryan) and Telugu (Telugu script; Dravidian)?
1.5 Objectives
The study aims to measure mean macro-F1 across budgets, identify the highest-mean method per cell, quantify resource use, and present all findings with their protocol limitations.
1.6 Contributions
The project provides a reproducible 108-run PEFT sweep, corrected seed-level validation summaries, resource measurements, and a clearly separated held-out hybrid follow-up.
1.7 Scope and Limitations
The scope is one encoder, one NLI task, two languages, and budgets up to 20,000 examples. The primary analysis uses validation data for learning-rate selection and reporting, so it is not an independent test claim.
1.8 Organization of the Report
Chapter 2 reviews related work. Chapter 3 presents the system and methodology. Chapter 4 summarizes compute use. Chapter 5 reports the validated primary results and the distinct hybrid test follow-up. Chapter 6 concludes and identifies future work. References and appendices follow.
2. LITERATURE REVIEW
2.1 PEFT
LoRA learns low-rank updates to selected frozen weights (Hu et al., 2021). DoRA extends this approach through magnitude–direction decomposition (Liu et al., 2024). IA³ instead learns small scaling vectors applied within transformer layers (Liu et al., 2022). These approaches make different trade-offs between adaptation capacity and trainable parameters.
2.2 LoRA, DoRA, and IA³
LoRA uses additive low-rank updates; DoRA separates a weight's magnitude and direction; IA³ learns multiplicative rescaling vectors. These mechanisms motivate an empirical comparison rather than assuming that a lower parameter count or a more elaborate decomposition will always improve task accuracy.
2.3 XLM-RoBERTa and IndicXNLI
XLM-RoBERTa is a multilingual encoder pretrained across many languages (Conneau et al., 2020). IndicXNLI extends natural-language inference evaluation to Indic languages, including Hindi and Telugu (Aggarwal et al., 2022). Prior PEFT comparisons have often used a fixed training size and predominantly Latin-script settings. This project jointly varies language and annotation budget, so its contribution is a controlled, descriptive comparison rather than a claim of universal PEFT superiority.
2.4 Existing Studies and Research Gap
Prior comparative PEFT studies motivate the present work but do not jointly test training-budget sensitivity and cross-script variation in this controlled setting. The research gap is therefore practical: whether one method ranking can be used across differing annotation budgets and Indic-language contexts. Existing controlled comparisons illustrate the value of reporting both accuracy and efficiency, but do not resolve this exact budget-and-script question (Nwaiwu, 2025; Nina et al., 2026).
3. SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
3.1 Research Design
The primary study is a balanced factorial experiment: 3 PEFT methods × 2 languages × 6 budgets × 3 random seeds = 108 validation runs. The budgets are 50, 100, 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 20,000 training examples. Macro-F1 is the central evaluation metric because IndicXNLI is a three-class classification task.
3.2 Dataset and Base Model
The dataset is IndicXNLI, restricted to Hindi and Telugu. The base model is XLM-RoBERTa-base with a sequence-classification head.
3.3 PEFT Methods and Experimental Design
The workflow validates the dataset and environment, preprocesses language-specific subsets, verifies the training infrastructure, selects one pooled learning rate per method, executes the full sweep, and aggregates seed-level results. The stored analysis uses the validation split and reports a two-sided t interval for three seeds (df = 2; t* = 4.302652729). The interval describes variability across seeds; it is not a pairwise significance test.
3.4 Training Procedure and Evaluation Metrics
Macro-F1 is the primary metric. Each method-language-budget cell is trained with three fixed seeds and results are aggregated as a mean with a two-sided t interval.
3.5 Experimental Pipeline and Reproducibility
Fixed random seeds: 42, 123, and 456 for every primary cell.
Versioned notebooks and CSV outputs record preprocessing, learning-rate search, training, and analysis.
Standard libraries: Python, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT, pandas, scikit-learn, NumPy, and Matplotlib.
Incremental experiment logging preserves per-run metric, memory, timing, and adapter metadata.
3.6 Software and Tools
Experiments were executed in Kaggle-style GPU environments using Python, PyTorch, Transformers, PEFT, Accelerate, pandas, scikit-learn, NumPy, Matplotlib, and Seaborn. The study uses XLM-RoBERTa-base, a sequence-classification head, and IndicXNLI Hindi and Telugu subsets.
3.7 Engineering Issues and Fixes
LoRA and DoRA use rank r = 8. IA³ uses learned scaling vectors. The pooled learning-rate search selected 1×10⁻⁴ for LoRA, 1×10⁻⁴ for DoRA, and 5×10⁻³ for IA³. All methods train the classification head alongside adapters. An infrastructure audit made this explicit through modules_to_save=['classifier']; this safeguard is important because a randomly initialized head must remain trainable for a valid sequence-classification comparison. The resulting corrected analysis is retained in the project outputs.
The training schedule varies by budget, so training budget and the total number of optimizer updates are not fully isolated. This trade-off should be considered when reading budget effects.
4. COMPUTATIONAL COST ANALYSIS
4.1 Compute Environment
No physical hardware was purchased for this project. Therefore, the relevant cost is GPU compute use. The recorded aggregate times below cover the primary sweep; Kaggle GPU access was treated as free-tier access. A monetary estimate, if required by the institution, should be calculated from the applicable cloud GPU hourly rate rather than inferred from these measurements.

Figure 1. Validation learning curves from the corrected primary analysis.
IA³ is the highest-mean method at 500, 1,000, and 2,000 examples in both languages. At 50 examples, DoRA has the highest mean in both languages; at 100 examples, DoRA leads in Hindi and IA³ in Telugu. At 20,000 examples, IA³ leads Hindi while LoRA leads Telugu. These results answer RQ1: PEFT ranking is budget-dependent. For RQ2, the intermediate-budget IA³ pattern is replicated across the two languages, but full cross-script ranking invariance is not supported because the smallest and largest budget cells differ.
5.2 Results by Language, Budget, and PEFT Ranking
The analysis flags runs at or within 0.001 of the one-class chance-accuracy baseline (approximately 0.3333) as near-baseline cases. They are retained rather than removed from the reported means and intervals. Of 108 runs, 24 (22.2%) meet this condition, indicating that the smallest budgets and some schedules are unstable.

Wide three-seed intervals and the retained near-baseline outcomes mean that the rankings should be treated as descriptive mean comparisons, not as definitive pairwise significance outcomes. IA³ uses a learning rate 50 times the selected LoRA/DoRA rate, which may contribute to small-budget sensitivity; the experiment does not isolate causality.

5.4 Comparison with Previous Work, Discussion, and Limitations
The evidence does not justify a single PEFT choice for every setting. IA³ is the strongest primary baseline family in the intermediate budgets, whereas DoRA or LoRA lead selected extreme low- and high-budget cells. The hybrid follow-up improves on the best primary method in a majority of tested cells, but its dual-learning-rate configuration was not tuned under the same protocol as the primary methods. It is therefore best described as promising supplemental evidence.
The absence of a broad DoRA advantage over LoRA is consistent with comparative PEFT findings in other settings, but this project is not powered to establish equivalence. The practical result is more modest: on this benchmark and configuration, added DoRA complexity did not yield a consistently higher mean score. This interpretation is consistent with the need to evaluate PEFT variants under the target task and resource budget rather than assuming a gain from architectural complexity alone (Liu et al., 2024; Nina et al., 2026).
6. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
6.1 Conclusion and Answers to Research Questions
This project compared LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ for Hindi and Telugu IndicXNLI classification across six annotation budgets. The controlled primary sweep shows that rankings depend on available data. IA³ is consistently the highest-mean method at the three intermediate budgets in both languages, but it is not the winner of every cell. Hence, a method ranking should be conditioned on budget and task context rather than assumed universal. The separate held-out hybrid study reports an 8/12-cell advantage over the best primary comparator, while requiring cautious interpretation because of tuning asymmetry.
6.2 Contributions, Limitations, and Future Work
Scale the study from 20,000 examples to the full available training data.
Use an untouched development/test protocol with per-language validation and preregistered comparison rules.
Evaluate additional Indic languages, scripts, and language families.
Repeat the comparison on other tasks, including generation and sequence labeling.
Test larger multilingual encoders and isolate the effect of the classification head and optimizer-update schedule.

A PROJECT REPORT ON
DOES PEFT METHOD RANKING HOLD ACROSS SCRIPT FAMILIES?
A Data-Efficiency Study on Low-Resource Indic Languages
Submitted by

CERTIFICATE
This is to certify that the project report entitled “Does PEFT Method Ranking Hold Across Script Families? A Data-Efficiency Study on Low-Resource Indic Languages” is a bona fide work carried out by [Your Name] ([Roll Number]) under my guidance. The work is submitted in partial fulfilment of the requirements for the award of the degree of [Degree Name] at [University / College Name].

Guide[Faculty Advisor Name][Designation]

ACKNOWLEDGEMENT
I express my sincere gratitude to my faculty advisor, [Faculty Advisor Name], for guidance and constructive feedback throughout this project. I also thank the Department of [Department Name], [University Name], and the open-source research community whose datasets and software made this study possible. I am grateful to my peers and family for their encouragement during the experimental and writing stages.
ABSTRACT
This study examines whether the relative ranking of parameter-efficient fine-tuning (PEFT) methods changes with labelled-data availability and remains stable across Indic script families. LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ were adapted to XLM-RoBERTa-base for IndicXNLI classification in Hindi and Telugu. A controlled sweep covered six training budgets (50–20,000 examples), three methods, two languages, and three random seeds, producing 108 validation runs. Mean macro-F1 rankings vary with budget: DoRA leads at 50 examples in both languages, IA³ leads at 500–2,000 examples in both languages and at 20,000 examples in Hindi, while LoRA leads at 20,000 examples in Telugu. Thus, no method is universally best. A separate held-out test follow-up compared a hybrid IA³+LoRA configuration with the best primary method in each cell; the hybrid won 8 of 12 cells. The results support budget-aware PEFT selection, while the small number of seeds, validation-set model selection, and asymmetric hybrid tuning limit inferential claims.

LIST OF ABBREVIATIONS
PEFT — Parameter-Efficient Fine-Tuning; LoRA — Low-Rank Adaptation; DoRA — Weight-Decomposed Low-Rank Adaptation; IA³ — Infused Adapter by Inhibiting and Amplifying Inner Activations; NLI — Natural Language Inference; GPU — Graphics Processing Unit.
1. INTRODUCTION
1.1 Background
Parameter-efficient fine-tuning adapts a large pretrained model while leaving most backbone weights frozen. It is attractive when compute, memory, or annotated examples are limited.
1.2 Problem Statement
A PEFT recommendation based on one language and one dataset size may not transfer to a different data regime or script. Existing comparisons seldom vary both axes together in a controlled Indic-language setting.
1.3 Motivation
Hindi and Telugu provide a useful contrast because they differ in script and language family while being evaluated with the same multilingual encoder and task. This makes it possible to investigate whether a ranking is robust or context-dependent.
1.4 Research Questions
This report addresses two research questions:
RQ1: Does the ranking of LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ change as the training-data budget changes?
RQ2: Is the observed ranking consistent for Hindi (Devanagari; Indo-Aryan) and Telugu (Telugu script; Dravidian)?
1.5 Objectives
The study aims to measure mean macro-F1 across budgets, identify the highest-mean method per cell, quantify resource use, and present all findings with their protocol limitations.
1.6 Contributions
The project provides a reproducible 108-run PEFT sweep, corrected seed-level validation summaries, resource measurements, and a clearly separated held-out hybrid follow-up.
1.7 Scope and Limitations
The scope is one encoder, one NLI task, two languages, and budgets up to 20,000 examples. The primary analysis uses validation data for learning-rate selection and reporting, so it is not an independent test claim.
1.8 Organization of the Report
Chapter 2 reviews related work. Chapter 3 presents the system and methodology. Chapter 4 summarizes compute use. Chapter 5 reports the validated primary results and the distinct hybrid test follow-up. Chapter 6 concludes and identifies future work. References and appendices follow.
2. LITERATURE REVIEW
2.1 PEFT
LoRA learns low-rank updates to selected frozen weights (Hu et al., 2021). DoRA extends this approach through magnitude–direction decomposition (Liu et al., 2024). IA³ instead learns small scaling vectors applied within transformer layers (Liu et al., 2022). These approaches make different trade-offs between adaptation capacity and trainable parameters.
2.2 LoRA, DoRA, and IA³
LoRA uses additive low-rank updates; DoRA separates a weight's magnitude and direction; IA³ learns multiplicative rescaling vectors. These mechanisms motivate an empirical comparison rather than assuming that a lower parameter count or a more elaborate decomposition will always improve task accuracy.
2.3 XLM-RoBERTa and IndicXNLI
XLM-RoBERTa is a multilingual encoder pretrained across many languages (Conneau et al., 2020). IndicXNLI extends natural-language inference evaluation to Indic languages, including Hindi and Telugu (Aggarwal et al., 2022). Prior PEFT comparisons have often used a fixed training size and predominantly Latin-script settings. This project jointly varies language and annotation budget, so its contribution is a controlled, descriptive comparison rather than a claim of universal PEFT superiority.
2.4 Existing Studies and Research Gap
Prior comparative PEFT studies motivate the present work but do not jointly test training-budget sensitivity and cross-script variation in this controlled setting. The research gap is therefore practical: whether one method ranking can be used across differing annotation budgets and Indic-language contexts.
3. SYSTEM DESIGN AND METHODOLOGY
3.1 Research Design
The primary study is a balanced factorial experiment: 3 PEFT methods × 2 languages × 6 budgets × 3 random seeds = 108 validation runs. The budgets are 50, 100, 500, 1,000, 2,000, and 20,000 training examples. Macro-F1 is the central evaluation metric because IndicXNLI is a three-class classification task.
3.2 Dataset and Base Model
The dataset is IndicXNLI, restricted to Hindi and Telugu. The base model is XLM-RoBERTa-base with a sequence-classification head.
3.3 PEFT Methods and Experimental Design
The workflow validates the dataset and environment, preprocesses language-specific subsets, verifies the training infrastructure, selects one pooled learning rate per method, executes the full sweep, and aggregates seed-level results. The stored analysis uses the validation split and reports a two-sided t interval for three seeds (df = 2; t* = 4.302652729). The interval describes variability across seeds; it is not a pairwise significance test.
3.4 Training Procedure and Evaluation Metrics
Macro-F1 is the primary metric. Each method-language-budget cell is trained with three fixed seeds and results are aggregated as a mean with a two-sided t interval.
3.5 Experimental Pipeline and Reproducibility
Fixed random seeds: 42, 123, and 456 for every primary cell.
Versioned notebooks and CSV outputs record preprocessing, learning-rate search, training, and analysis.
Standard libraries: Python, PyTorch, Hugging Face Transformers, PEFT, pandas, scikit-learn, NumPy, and Matplotlib.
Incremental experiment logging preserves per-run metric, memory, timing, and adapter metadata.
3.6 Software and Tools
Experiments were executed in Kaggle-style GPU environments using Python, PyTorch, Transformers, PEFT, Accelerate, pandas, scikit-learn, NumPy, Matplotlib, and Seaborn. The study uses XLM-RoBERTa-base, a sequence-classification head, and IndicXNLI Hindi and Telugu subsets.
3.7 Engineering Issues and Fixes
LoRA and DoRA use rank r = 8. IA³ uses learned scaling vectors. The pooled learning-rate search selected 1×10⁻⁴ for LoRA, 1×10⁻⁴ for DoRA, and 5×10⁻³ for IA³. All methods train the classification head alongside adapters. An infrastructure audit made this explicit through modules_to_save=['classifier']; this safeguard is important because a randomly initialized head must remain trainable for a valid sequence-classification comparison. The resulting corrected analysis is retained in the project outputs.
The training schedule varies by budget, so training budget and the total number of optimizer updates are not fully isolated. This trade-off should be considered when reading budget effects.
4. COMPUTATIONAL COST ANALYSIS
4.1 Compute Environment
No physical hardware was purchased for this project. Therefore, the relevant cost is GPU compute use. The recorded aggregate times below cover the primary sweep; Kaggle GPU access was treated as free-tier access. A monetary estimate, if required by the institution, should be calculated from the applicable cloud GPU hourly rate rather than inferred from these measurements.

Figure 1. Validation learning curves from the corrected primary analysis.
IA³ is the highest-mean method at 500, 1,000, and 2,000 examples in both languages. At 50 examples, DoRA has the highest mean in both languages; at 100 examples, DoRA leads in Hindi and IA³ in Telugu. At 20,000 examples, IA³ leads Hindi while LoRA leads Telugu. These results answer RQ1: PEFT ranking is budget-dependent. For RQ2, the intermediate-budget IA³ pattern is replicated across the two languages, but full cross-script ranking invariance is not supported because the smallest and largest budget cells differ.
5.2 Results by Language, Budget, and PEFT Ranking
The analysis flags runs at or within 0.001 of the one-class chance-accuracy baseline (approximately 0.3333) as near-baseline cases. They are retained rather than removed from the reported means and intervals. Of 108 runs, 24 (22.2%) meet this condition, indicating that the smallest budgets and some schedules are unstable.

5.4 Comparison with Previous Work, Discussion, and Limitations
The evidence does not justify a single PEFT choice for every setting. IA³ is the strongest primary baseline family in the intermediate budgets, whereas DoRA or LoRA lead selected extreme low- and high-budget cells. The hybrid follow-up improves on the best primary method in a majority of tested cells, but its dual-learning-rate configuration was not tuned under the same protocol as the primary methods. It is therefore best described as promising supplemental evidence.
The absence of a broad DoRA advantage over LoRA is consistent with comparative PEFT findings in other settings, but this project is not powered to establish equivalence. The practical result is more modest: on this benchmark and configuration, added DoRA complexity did not yield a consistently higher mean score.
6. CONCLUSION AND FUTURE WORK
6.1 Conclusion and Answers to Research Questions
This project compared LoRA, DoRA, and IA³ for Hindi and Telugu IndicXNLI classification across six annotation budgets. The controlled primary sweep shows that rankings depend on available data. IA³ is consistently the highest-mean method at the three intermediate budgets in both languages, but it is not the winner of every cell. Hence, a method ranking should be conditioned on budget and task context rather than assumed universal. The separate held-out hybrid study reports an 8/12-cell advantage over the best primary comparator, while requiring cautious interpretation because of tuning asymmetry.
6.2 Contributions, Limitations, and Future Work
Scale the study from 20,000 examples to the full available training data.
Use an untouched development/test protocol with per-language validation and preregistered comparison rules.
Evaluate additional Indic languages, scripts, and language families.
Repeat the comparison on other tasks, including generation and sequence labeling.
Test larger multilingual encoders and isolate the effect of the classification head and optimizer-update schedule.
